title: Sort Integers by the Power Value
description: Sort integers in a range by their Collatz-style power value, ties broken by value, using memoized simulation and a composite sort key.

sections.title: Sort Integers by the Power Value

content.title: Sort Integers by the Power Value

blocks.text: The power of an integer x is the number of steps needed to transform it into 1, where each step replaces x with x/2 if x is even, or 3x+1 if x is odd. Given integers lo, hi, and k, sort all integers in [lo, hi] by increasing power, breaking ties by increasing value, and return the k-th integer (1-indexed) in that order.

blocks.caption: Each number's power is computed by simulating its chain to 1, then the whole range is sorted by that power.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Field","Details"],"rows":[["Input","lo, hi (inclusive range), k (1-indexed rank to return)"],["Power rule","Even: x = x/2. Odd: x = 3x+1. Count steps until x reaches 1"],["Sort order","By power ascending, ties broken by value ascending"],["Output","The k-th integer in that sorted order"]]}

blocks.text: This is another "sort by a derived property, with a value tiebreaker" problem, the same shape as Sort Array By Increasing Frequency, but here the derived property (power) requires an actual simulation to compute rather than a simple count.

blocks.title: Connection
blocks.text: Since the power computation for a large x often passes through smaller values already computed (or about to be computed) for other numbers in the range, memoization can avoid redundant work across different starting numbers.

Picture every integer in the range as a racer, following the Collatz-style rule (halve if even, triple-plus-one if odd) until reaching 1. Each racer's "power" is how many steps it took. Racers are ranked by fewest steps first, and ties are broken by the smaller starting number.

blocks.caption: Racers following the same rule finish in different numbers of steps.

items: Compute the power of every integer from lo to hi by directly simulating the chain until reaching 1.
Sort the range using a composite key: (power, value).
Return the k-th element (1-indexed) of that sorted order.

blocks.title: Answer
blocks.text: Sorted by power ascending, then value ascending for ties: [12, 13, 14, 15] (12 and 13 tie at power 9, sorted by value; 14 and 15 tie at power 17). The 2nd element (k=2) is 13, matching the expected output.

The direct approach recomputes each number's power from scratch via simulation, which is correct but can repeat a lot of work: many different starting numbers in the range converge onto the SAME smaller values partway through their chains.

Memoizing power(x) means that once any number's chain passes through a value already computed (either from a prior number in the range, or from earlier in the same chain), the remaining steps are looked up instantly instead of resimulated.
Simulate each number's power independently (no memoization), then sort the range using a manual comparison sort applying the (power, value) ordering rule.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Metric","Value","Why"],"rows":[["Time","O((hi - lo) * (S + log(hi - lo)))","S is the average chain length per number, resimulated from scratch each time, plus a bubble sort"],["Space","O(hi - lo)","The array of (value, power) pairs"]]}

blocks.title: Bottleneck
blocks.text: Recomputing power from scratch for every number, with no reuse of shared chain suffixes, and a quadratic sort, both do unnecessary work.

Memoize power(x) in a hash map: whenever a chain reaches a value already computed, return the cached result immediately instead of continuing the simulation. Sort the range using a built-in efficient sort with a composite (power, value) key.

items: Compute power(x) recursively, caching results in a memo map so overlapping chain suffixes are only computed once total.
Sort the range with a comparator using the cached power values, O((hi-lo) log(hi-lo)).

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Time","Space"],"rows":[["Brute Force, no memoization + bubble sort","O((hi-lo) * S + (hi-lo)^2)","O(hi - lo)"],["Optimized, memoized power + efficient sort","O((hi-lo) * (S + log(hi-lo)))","O(hi - lo + cache size)"]]}

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: Memoization mainly helps when chains from different numbers converge onto shared values, reducing redundant simulation; the efficient sort removes the quadratic sorting cost.

items: When a derived property requires simulation to compute (not just a lookup or count), memoization avoids recomputing shared chain suffixes across different inputs.
A composite sort key (primary property, then value as tiebreaker) is the standard way to encode "sort by X, ties broken by Y."
This Collatz-style chain-length property appears in several classic problems and always benefits from caching intermediate results.

blocks.text: Sort Integers by the Power Value is solved by computing each integer's power via simulation (memoized to avoid recomputing shared chain suffixes), then sorting the range with a composite key of (power, value) and returning the k-th element.
